title: Open-source platform for kinematic analysis of mouse forelimb movement
author: Berezhnoi, Chehade, et al.

steps.title: Assemble breakout board
steps.instruction: Build the behavioral‑box control board in a 3‑D‑printed enclosure using a breadboard and an Arduino Nano as the core controller.

substeps.instruction: Position two Adafruit AT424QT1070 capacitive touch sensor boards, a ULN2003 stepper‑motor driver, and an IR proximity sensor on the breadboard and solder them in place (Figure 3A).
Connect each component to the 10‑pin 2.54 mm sockets (pins 6, 7) as shown; all power (red) and ground (brown) wires must converge on the single 5 V power/ground pins of the Arduino socket.

Optional: modify the IR proximity sensor for contrast/beam‑break detection by unsoldering its two LEDs, mounting one IR emitter at the bottom of the slit and the detector at the top, then resoldering or using pin‑socket wires.

Solder the three relay cables: a 10‑pin connector for the breadboard interface, a 4‑pin connector for the feeder stepper motor, and a simple breadboard with two buttons for manual feeder control (see Figure 3A‑1,2,3).
Mount the Arduino Nano on the same breadboard (or nearby) and make the button cables longer and more durable.
Connect the control board to the behavioral‑box sensors according to the diagram in Figure 3A and link the camera: Arduino pin 12 → camera pin 1 (GPIO) and Arduino GND → camera pin 6 (GND).

steps.title: Configure Arduino and upload program
steps.instruction: Install the Arduino development environment, select a behavioral program, and upload it to the Nano so it runs autonomously on power‑up.

substeps.instruction: Download the Arduino IDE from https://www.arduino.cc/en/software.
Connect the Arduino Nano to the computer via USB and launch the IDE.

Choose one of the provided sketches from the repository (e.g., Reaching_Task_Manual) or modify a script to suit experimental needs; other options include Reaching_Task_Draft, Reaching_Task_Feeder_Training, Reaching_Task_Door_Training, and Reaching_Task_CS_Training.
Upload the selected sketch; note that after a single upload the board will execute that program on every power‑up. To change protocols, reconnect to the computer and upload a different sketch.

steps.title: Set up data streaming and recording
steps.instruction: Install required Python tools, configure the FLIR Blackfly S camera, and run the provided scripts to record synchronized video and sensor data.

substeps.instruction: Locate the Python scripts in the repository (e.g., Reaching_Task_VAI/Recordingtoolbox/FLIR_GPU/CameraRoll.py) and copy them to an easy‑access folder.

Install Anaconda Python, the FLIR Spinnaker SDK, and the PySpin API (download the appropriate Spinnaker version from FLIR, then install Anaconda and finally the matching "Latest Python Spinnaker" package).

Add required Python libraries: run `pip install scikit-video` in the Anaconda Prompt, and download the FFMPEG executable (https://ffmpeg.org/download.html); edit the script line `skvideo.setFFmpegPath('C:/path_where_you_put_ffmpeg/bin/')` to point to the folder you created.
Connect both the Arduino board and the FLIR Blackfly S camera to USB ports (camera must be in a USB 3.0 port to avoid dropped frames).

Start recording by executing the script, e.g., `python C:/folder_with_a_script/CameraRoll.py`. The script streams compressed video, saves it to the specified folder, and writes sensor data (touch, position, trial timing) as a table aligned with frame numbers.
Critical: verify that the camera‑sync pin (Arduino pin 12) is correctly wired to the camera’s GPIO pin 1 and that the output folder path is set correctly in the script.

steps.title: Install analysis software environment
steps.instruction: Set up a dedicated Anaconda environment with DeepLabCut, Anipose, and all other dependencies required for the kinematic analysis notebooks.

substeps.instruction: Download the repository scripts and Jupyter notebooks from https://github.com/BerezhnoyD/Reaching_Task_VAI (also archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7383917).
If not already installed, download and install Anaconda Python (https://www.anaconda.com/products/distribution).
From the repository, obtain the `DEEPLABCUT.yml` file that lists all required packages, including DeepLabCut and Anipose.
Create the environment by running `conda env create -f DEEPLABCUT.yml` in an Anaconda Prompt.
Activate the new environment: `conda activate DEEPLABCUT` and launch Jupyter Notebook (`jupyter notebook`).
The notebooks will appear in the browser; they are organized as Notebook 1 (tracking), Notebook 2 (analysis/labeling), and Notebook 3 (visualization).

steps.title: Conduct mouse reach training schedule
steps.instruction: Run the behavioral protocol consisting of habituation, shaping, and training sessions while maintaining the specified feeding schedule.

substeps.instruction: Habituation: 5 consecutive days of exposure to the reaching box.
Shaping: 2–3 days of progressive assistance to encourage reaching.
Training: 7 days of full‑task trials.
All sessions are performed during the light phase; schedule experiments to finish ~1 h before the start of the dark phase.
Mice are motivated by a 16‑hour food deprivation; feed them ~1 h before the dark phase.
Use 5 mg sugar pellets (≈2 mm diameter) as the reward.

steps.title: Track videos and triangulate 3D trajectories
steps.instruction: Process raw FLIR videos with DeepLabCut and Anipose to obtain calibrated 3‑D paw trajectories.

substeps.instruction: Open `ReachOut - Tracking.ipynb` (Notebook 1).
Cell 1: Split each acquired video into left, central, and right views using the provided cropping script (apply to both behavior and calibration videos).
Cell 2: Launch the DeepLabCut GUI; load the split videos, label the points of interest (snout, palm, four fingers, pellet), train the network, evaluate performance, and generate tracking results.
Save the tracking output as `*.csv` tables for each view (central and mirror).
Optional: run the 2‑D tracking notebook instead of the full pipeline if desired.
For best accuracy, run DeepLabCut twice—once on the frontal view and once on the mirror view—creating two separate networks.

Cell 3‑4: Triangulate the 2‑D points with Anipose. First, calibrate the camera system using a checkerboard video (4 × 4 squares, each 1 × 1 mm) recorded right before each session; the script detects the pattern and creates `calibration.toml`.
Apply the calibration file to the DeepLabCut `*.h5` files from both views to compute 3‑D coordinates; specify the three input files and an output path.
The result is a `*.csv` file containing absolute 3‑D coordinates (mm) for each tracked point, which can be visually inspected to confirm correct reconstruction.

steps.title: Analyze and label reach trajectories
steps.instruction: Extract individual reaches from the 3‑D data, assign behavioral categories, and generate a scalar data frame.

substeps.instruction: Open `ReachOut - Analysis.ipynb` (Notebook 2).

Run the `tracking_split` script: a GUI loads the `*.csv` file, displays the full trajectory, and lets you scroll (500‑frame windows). Use the red span selector on the side‑view plots to mark a single reach, then click the green “Save” button to store it.
Repeat for all reaches in the file; when finished click the green “Save_all” button to export the full set of extracted reaches as an `*.h5` file.

Run the `viewer` script: it loads the `*.h5` file and the corresponding `*.mp4` video, shows the trajectory from multiple views, and provides two dropdown menus—one to select a trajectory and one to assign a reach type.
Classify each reach into one of six categories: Grasped, Missed, Flicked, Lost, In‑vain, or Artifact. Close the video with the ‘Q’ key after labeling.
The script saves a `*_scalar.h5` file containing kinematic parameters (duration, velocity, endpoint, etc.) for every labeled reach.

steps.title: Visualize kinematic data and clustering
steps.instruction: Generate plots of average trajectories, scalar parameters, and optional clustering results using the final notebook.

substeps.instruction: Open `ReachOut - Visualization.ipynb` (Notebook 3).

Run `reach_view`: select a reach category from the dropdown; the script displays the mean 3‑D trajectory with projections onto X (forward), Y (sideward), and Z (upward) axes. Right‑click to save the figure.
Run `scalar_view`: choose a category and a kinematic parameter; the left panel shows individual reach values with the mean, the right panel shows the mean ± standard deviation.
Optional: run `clustering` to apply a chosen clustering algorithm to the scalar data; results are added as a new label column in the `*_scalar.h5` file and can be visualized.
Run the final script to display the count of reaches in each behavioral category.
